title: Argentina Runs on QR Codes Now, Not Crisp Hundred Dollar Bills
summary: Most tourist money advice about Argentina is outdated. Here are the mistakes visitors still make with cash, cards, and exchange rates, and how QR payments fix most of them.
body_markdown:
Ask five people how to handle money in Argentina and you will get five confident answers, most of them a few years out of date. Argentina's money situation changes faster than guidebooks, faster than Reddit threads, and definitely faster than that friend who visited once and now gives lectures about it.


So let's go through the actual mistakes visitors keep making in 2026, and what locals in Buenos Aires, Mendoza, and Salta are really doing at the counter.


## The old advice: fly in with an envelope of US dollars


For years, the standard tourist move was to arrive with a stack of crisp hundred dollar bills, find a cueva or a friend-of-a-friend, and swap them at a far better rate than any bank would give. That advice made sense once. Argentina has long had a gap between the official exchange rate and other rates, and visitors heard about it constantly.


The problem is that the landscape keeps shifting. The gap between rates grows, shrinks, and moves around, and card and digital payments have been given rates specifically designed to be competitive for foreigners. Many visitors still land with a fat envelope of cash, go through the stress of exchanging it, and end up with no meaningful advantage over someone who just paid digitally.


The real mistake is not the dollars themselves. It is building your entire trip around a cash strategy from a different era, then carrying the consequences around in your pockets.


## The peso stack problem nobody warns you about


Here is what the envelope strategy actually gets you: a brick of pesos. Inflation means prices are high in nominal terms, and even with larger denomination notes in circulation, paying for a nice dinner in cash can mean counting out a small ritual of bills while the waiter waits politely.


Tourists then make the second mistake, which is exchanging too much at once. Pesos lose value while they sit in your money belt. Locals know this, which is exactly why so many of them have moved their daily spending onto their phones. If you exchange a big amount on day one of a three week trip, you are voluntarily taking on the inflation that Argentines spend their lives trying to dodge.


If you do carry cash, exchange small amounts, often. Better yet, keep most of your money digital and convert at the moment you pay.


## Ignoring the QR code sitting on every counter


This is the big one. Walk into almost any cafe, kiosco, verdulería, or parrilla in Argentina and there is a QR code at the register, usually for[Mercado Pago](https://moretapay.com/networks/mercado-pago) , often[MODO](https://moretapay.com/networks/modo) as well. Watch the locals: they scan, confirm, and leave. No bill counting, no change, no drama.


Argentina quietly became one of the most QR-native countries in Latin America, in the same way Brazil did with[Pix](https://moretapay.com/networks/pix) next door. (We covered


[what tourists get wrong about paying in Brazil](https://moretapay.com/blog/cash-card-or-pix-what-tourists-get-wrong-about-paying-in-brazil-2026-11-11)


recently, and the pattern is strikingly similar.)


Tourists mostly watch this from the outside, because Mercado Pago and MODO are built around Argentine bank accounts and local ID. The assumption is: no local account, no QR payments for me, back to the cash stack.


That assumption is now wrong. With Moreta Pay you top up a wallet from your own bank or card at home, in your own currency, then scan the same Mercado Pago or MODO QR codes everyone else is scanning. The app shows you the amount, the merchant name, and the exchange rate before you confirm, the wallet converts to pesos, and the merchant is paid instantly. You are inside the local system without a local bank account.


## Guessing at exchange rates instead of reading them


Argentina's multiple-rate history has trained visitors into two opposite errors. Some assume any card or digital payment uses a terrible official rate and insist on cash for everything. Others assume digital is always the best deal and never check.


Both are guesses. The honest answer is that rates in Argentina move, and the only reliable habit is to look at the actual rate you are getting at the moment you pay. This is where opaque card statements hurt you, because you find out the rate days later, after the bank has added whatever foreign transaction fee it felt like adding.


Paying by QR through Moreta Pay flips that around: the FX rate is on screen before you confirm, with no hidden foreign transaction fees stacked on afterward. If the number looks good, pay. If it ever does not, you still have the option to pay another way. Information before the payment, not after, is the whole game in Argentina.


## Treating ATM runs as a plan


Argentine ATMs are famous among travelers for low withdrawal limits and fees that sting, especially relative to how quickly a stack of pesos disappears into dinners and taxis. Some visitors structure whole afternoons around finding a machine with cash in it.


If your card refunds foreign ATM fees, occasional withdrawals for small purchases are fine, and it is worth


[checking whether your debit card actually refunds ATM fees abroad](https://moretapay.com/blog/how-to-check-whether-your-debit-card-refunds-atm-fees-abroad)


before you leave. But as a primary strategy, ATM runs in Argentina mean paying fees repeatedly for the privilege of holding a depreciating currency. Keep a modest cash reserve for the handful of places that are genuinely cash-only, like some taxis, small town markets, and tips, and do the rest by QR.


## A sane money setup for an Argentina trip


Pulling it together, here is what works in 2026:


- **Before you fly:**


set up your wallet and top it up from your home bank (Plaid or ACH from the US, SEPA from Europe, Faster Payments from the UK, e-Transfer from Canada) or an international card. Do this at home, calmly, not on airport Wi-Fi.


- **Carry a little cash, not a brick:**


enough pesos for a day or two of small stuff. Replenish in small amounts.


- **Default to QR:**


if there is a Mercado Pago or MODO code at the counter, scan it. Check the rate on screen, confirm, done.


- **Use QR online too:**


booking platforms and shopping sites that accept QR-based payment can come out of the same wallet, so a hotel in Bariloche and an empanada in San Telmo draw from one balance.


- **Watch the rate, every time:**


never assume. Read the number before confirming. In Argentina, that single habit outperforms every clever strategy from five years ago.


The tourists who struggle in Argentina are the ones fighting the last war: hoarding dollars, hoarding pesos, hunting ATMs. The ones who enjoy it are paying the way porteños pay, one scan at a time, with the exchange rate in plain sight.
